power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

live_data_statements: Conversely, if the target word mismatched the stress pattern produced in the auditory prime (e.g., prinCIpio "beginning" following the PRINci-prime), participants were slower relative to the control condition.
To explore this possibility, participants completed two modules of the Profiles of Musical Perception Skills (PROMS) test (Law & Zentner, 2012; Strauss et al., 2024).
A total of 90 participants aged between 18 and 40 (42 female, 46 male, 2 other; M Age = 28.69, SD = 4.85, range: 21-40) was recruited through Prolific (https://www.prolific.com/).
All participants were native speakers of Spanish, born in Spain, and self-reported to be located in Spain while taking part in the study.
For both sessions, participants provided informed consent as approved by the [ethics assessment committee, redacted for review].
These participants were subsequently excluded from the main audiovisual experiment.
Participants were asked to respond by pressing the space bar when they encountered a catch trial.
After participants provided consent, they were asked to adjust the audio volume to a comfortable level.

Since the two verb forms of the minimal pair are each congruent with a different subject (1st vs. 3rd person singular), we asked our participants to indicate which pronoun (yo "I" or ella "she", congruent with clasiFIco or clasifiCÓ, respectively) they thought fit best with the sentence.
Participants had the option to respond at any time once the video stimulus started playing, ensuring the collection of very sensitive response times.
If a response had not been provided during the video phase, the trial continued to a blank answer screen, where participants had another 3000 ms to respond.
Participants were instructed to press F for a yo-response, J for an ella-response, and the spacebar whenever they encountered a catch trial.
Four participants were removed from the data set because they failed to provide accurate responses to more than one third of the catch trials.

As acoustic markers of stress gradually changed from indicating stress on the penultimate, to stress on the last syllable, participants were ever less likely to select the pronoun matching the penultimate stress pattern.

Importantly, it is unlikely that the participants were unable to determine where the gesture was aligned at all, given the difference in response times between beat alignment conditions (discussed below in greater detail).

For example, it has been shown that questions are answered faster if they are accompanied by semantically constraining gestures (including iconic and deictic gestures; Holler et al., 2018; ter Bekke et al., 2024), and that participants were faster at indicating whether they felt addressed or not when a stimulus was combined with an iconic gesture (Nagels et al., 2015).

With respect to lexical access, it has been shown that participants were faster to relate primes and targets when the stimuli contained iconic gestures and speech that matched, rather than mismatched (Kelly et al., 2010).

The effect of Sentence Context was significant (β = 2.355, SE = 0.308, z = 7.649, p < .001), indicating that participants were more likely to select the yoresponse (the pronoun congruent with the present-tense verb form) when the sentence context contained a bias to the present tense, and less likely to respond with yo when the sentence context contained a bias to the past tense.

text.text: Next to acoustic cues, lexical stress can be communicated visually through the timing of beat gestures.
This study investigated for the first time how auditory and visual lexical stress cues are weighted in meaningful sentences.
Minimal stress pairs of Spanish verb forms (clasiFIco, "I classify" vs. clasifiCÓ, "(s)he classified") were embedded in sentence contexts that biased towards either member of the pair.
Stress was manipulated acoustically along a continuum, and visually by aligning a beat gesture to the penultimate or last syllable.
Native listeners selected the pronoun (yo "I" or ella "she") they felt fit best with the sentence.
Listeners were sensitive to acoustic cues, as indicated by both responses and response times.
While gesture alignment did not significantly affect pronoun selection, response times were shorter when the gesture matched the semantic context bias.
This study thus shows that in full sentences, congruent (vs. incongruent) gestural timing affects word recognition.
In face-to-face speech comprehension, a listener is tasked with combining rich acoustic and visual signals in the context of a discourse (Holler & Levinson, 2019).

text.text: This study addressed these limitations, investigating the audiovisual perception of lexical stress in full, meaningful sentences with semantic constraints.
In particular, this study examined the relative contribution of acoustic, visual, and abstract linguistic cues to the perception of lexical stress.
To do so, acoustic and gestural markers of stress were independently manipulated for Spanish verb forms, which were embedded in semantically constraining sentences.
That is, these sentences contained an initial adverbial phrase providing a semantic cue for one specific stress pattern on the verb form.
This way, the current study tested how multimodal components of the speech signal are weighted and integrated with each other, and with predictions generated by preceding sentence context.
Moreover, the use of an audiovisual paradigm with full sentences offers a better representation of natural communication.
Lexical stress refers to the relative prominence of one syllable in a word, compared to the other syllables in that word (Cutler & Jesse, 2021; Cutler, 2005).

text.text: In free-stress languages, such as English, Dutch, and Spanish, the stressed syllable of a word is not restricted to a specific position in that word.
As a result, these languages allow minimal lexical stress pairs, in which words differ only in the position of lexical stress (e.g., English OBject vs. obJECT, where capital letters denote stress).
In these cases, stress is an essential cue to the lexical identity of a word.
Also apart from minimal pairs, stress provides useful information to the identity of the word.

Indeed, corpus analyses on English, Dutch and Spanish show that including lexical stress information reduces the number of lexical items embedded in other words (Cutler et al., 2004; Cutler & Pasveer, 2006; Van Heuven & Hagman, 1988).

However, this 'embedding rate' drops drastically to 0.73 stress is taken into account (e.g., CAra "face" is not an embedded competitor of caraMElo "caramel" if stress is considered; Cutler et al., 2004).

text.text: Lexical stress information may therefore be used in word disambiguation, facilitating speech comprehension.
Indeed, several behavioural experiments have shown that lexical stress is immediately taken into account during speech perception.

Even for isolated syllables, Dutch and Spanish listeners have been shown to perform above chance when instructed to decide whether a spliced-out syllable is stressed or not (Cutler & Van Donselaar, 2001; Torreira et al., 2014).

text.text: Listeners of these two languages were also faster to respond in lexical decision tasks when they were offered an auditory prime that matched the target in stress pattern, than when the target and prime mismatched (Soto-Faraco et al., 2001; Van Donselaar et al., 2005).

text.text: For example, when Spanish participants heard the fragment PRINci-(/ˈpɾin.θi/) as the acoustic prime, they were faster to respond to the visually presented PRINcipe "prince", compared to when an unrelated control condition was offered as the auditory prime.

text.text: Beat gestures are brief, biphasic movements of the hand that occur very frequently in natural communication and are used to convey emphasis rather than semantic meaning (McNeill, 1992; Shattuck-Hufnagel & Ren, 2018).
text.formatted: Beat gestures are brief, biphasic movements of the hand that occur very frequently in natural communication and are used to convey emphasis rather than semantic meaning <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(McNeill, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Shattuck-Hufnagel & Ren, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Beat gestures tightly align temporally with accentuated words and syllables (Leonard & Cummins, 2011; Krahmer & Swerts, 2007), allowing listeners to use them as a cue to both phrasal and lexical stress in speech perception (Krahmer & Swerts, 2007; Bujok et al., 2025; Rohrer et al., 2025; Bosker & Peeters, 2021).

text.text: Indeed, beat gestures can attract lexical stress perception to the syllable during which the gesture is produced (Bosker & Peeters, 2021; Bujok et al., 2025; Rohrer et al., 2025).

text.text: For example, when presented with identical acoustic tokens, a Spanish listener is more likely to perceive HAblo "I speak" with initial stress when the apex of the gesture (the point of maximal extension of the hand) is aligned to the first syllable of the word.
Conversely, when it is aligned to the second syllable, the listener is more likely to perceive haBLÓ "(s)he spoke" with final stress (Rohrer et al., 2025).

text.text: Moreover, when the difference in acoustic prominence between the stressed and unstressed syllables is less pronounced, the effect of the beat gesture on lexical stress perception is even larger (Bujok et al., 2025; Rohrer et al., 2025; Maran et al., 2025) and more consistent within listeners over time (Cos et al., 2024).

text.text: Beat gestures thus seem to provide reliable evidence to the location of lexical stress, complementing that of the acoustic signalespecially when the acoustic signal is less reliable.
These studies on beat gestures investigated stress perception in a multimodal, and therefore more naturalistic setting compared to a speech-only situation.
Nevertheless, research on audiovisual stress perception so far remains limited in that it focused on isolated words or words in carrier sentences only (e.g., "Now I say…").
It therefore remains unclear to what extent beat gestures influence lexical stress perception in more naturalistic sentences.
Moreover, in addition to acoustic and visual markers of lexical stress, it is possible that stress processing is also affected by abstract linguistic predictions generated from the sentence context.
In Spanish, for example, the minimal stress pair clasiFIco / clasifiCÓ "I classify / (s)he classified" represents a difference in verb tense.

A sentence starting with a reference to a specific point in time (e.g., anoche "last night") may cause the listener to be more expectant of a verb form with a corresponding tense (i.e., clasifiCÓ), affecting the processing of the subsequent acoustic and visual signal of the verb form itself.

The current study addressed these issues, first asking what role beat gestures play in lexical stress perception for words that are embedded in complete utterances and second, how the effect of acoustic and visual cues to stress interacts with prior semantic constraints.

To interpret the relative contribution of acoustic and visual markers of stress on the one hand, and the importance of predictions from the sentence context on the other, the current study adopted a cue integration framework proposed by Martin (2016).
text.formatted: To interpret the relative contribution of acoustic and visual markers of stress on the one hand, and the importance of predictions from the sentence context on the other, the current study adopted a cue integration framework proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Martin (2016)</ref>.

text.text: In this framework, cues of different levels of linguistic representation are combined after weighing them according to their estimated reliability in the current situation.

The model assumes that lower-level ('signalbased') cues (e.g., the acoustic signal, phonemes and words) and higher-level, abstract cues (ranging from phrase structure to discourse context, pragmatic meaning and world knowledge) interact with each other to bias the processing of the upcoming speech signal.

As such, the model is particularly suited for interpreting the role of semantic context (an abstract linguistic cue) and its effect on the subsequent processing of acoustic and gestural information (signal-based cues).

While the framework has received support from both behavioural (Kaufeld, Naumann, et al., 2020; Kaufeld, Ravenschlag, et al., 2020; S. W. Y. Li et al., 2026) and neuroimaging studies (e.g., Bai et al., 2022; Martin, 2018), the current study is the first to apply the framework to visual cues (i.e., signal-based cues from a different modality).

text.text: Finally, at least for words in isolation, it has been shown that audiovisual lexical stress perception is subject to considerable individual variability.
Some listeners appear to primarily weigh the auditory component, while others are guided to a larger extent by gestural information (Cos et al., 2024; Rohrer et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Some listeners appear to primarily weigh the auditory component, while others are guided to a larger extent by gestural information <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cos et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Rohrer et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This individual variation does not seem to correlate with measures of phonological or visual working memory (Rohrer et al., 2025).

text.text: By means of exploration, the current study tested the role of musical aptitude as another potential source of individual variation.
Previous research has demonstrated a relationship between musical skills and prosodic perception (for a meta-analysis, see Jansen et al., 2023).

text.text: Some studies have even suggested that music and speech processing use shared mechanisms (e.g., Perrachione et al., 2013).

text.text: Given the acoustic properties of lexical stress and the rhythmic nature of beat gestures, it is possible that measures of musicality can indeed be correlated with acoustic or visual effects in lexical stress perception.

The current study tested whether the timing of a beat gesture affects the perception of lexical stress for words that are embedded in semantically constraining or unconstraining full Spanish sentences.
Spanish is a pro-drop language, usually omitting the pronoun marking the subject.
Moreover, all regular verbs ending in -ar contain several minimal stress pairs (e.g., clasiFIco vs. clasifiCÓ), making lexical stress perception exceptionally relevant.

Beat gestures were aligned to the main verb form of a sentence (e.g., En este momento, clasifico las plantas según su tipo, "In this moment, I classify the plants according to their type", with the verb form marked in boldface), presented as an audiovisual stimulus.

Through video and audio editing, we manipulated the acoustic cues to lexical stress (creating a continuum ranging from clasiFIco "I classify" to clasifiCÓ "(s)he classified"), as well as the alignment of a beat gesture to either the penultimate syllable or the last syllable.

Finally, the semantic content of the initial phrase of the sentence varied, providing a bias to a present-tense reading (e.g., En este momento "at the moment"), past-tense reading (e.g., El pasado abril "last april") or no-tense bias in particular (e.g., Diligentemente "diligently", serving as a baseline condition).
The semantic content of the sentence context thus served as an abstract linguistic cue.

Most studies on audiovisual stress perception asked participants which member of the minimal pair they perceived (i.e., HAblo or haBLÓ; Rohrer et al., 2025; see also Bujok et al., 2025; Bosker & Peeters, 2021; Leal-Arenas & Huensch, 2024).
text.formatted: Most studies on audiovisual stress perception asked participants which member of the minimal pair they perceived (i.e., HAblo or haBLÓ; <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Rohrer et al., 2025</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Bujok et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Bosker & Peeters, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Leal-Arenas & Huensch, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The current study adopted a different task to avoid drawing explicit attention to the verb form, which may lead listeners to boost the weighting of the local acoustic and visual cues relative to the context bias cue.
In the current study, participants therefore responded to the stimuli by selecting the pronoun that they thought "fit best with the sentence", choosing between yo "I" and ella "she".
In addition to these categorisation responses, response times were collected as a sensitive online measure of processing efficiency related to cue integration.

The independent manipulation of acoustic, visual, and semantic cues allowed for the examination of the interplay and relative weighting of each combination of cues, as well as the formulation of a hypothesis for each cue by itself.

With respect to the acoustic continuum, we expected to observe a gradual decrease in the likelihood of a yo-response being given when the audio changed stepwise from stress on the penultimate syllable (e.g., clasiFIco "I classify", congruent with yo) to stress on the last syllable (clasifiCÓ, incongruent with yo and congruent with ella; Rohrer et al., 2025; Bujok et al., 2025; Bosker & Peeters, 2021).
text.formatted: With respect to the acoustic continuum, we expected to observe a gradual decrease in the likelihood of a yo-response being given when the audio changed stepwise from stress on the penultimate syllable (e.g., clasiFIco "I classify", congruent with yo) to stress on the last syllable (clasifiCÓ, incongruent with yo and congruent with ella; <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Rohrer et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Bujok et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Bosker & Peeters, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In terms of response times, we expected that clear audio would elicit faster responses than ambiguous (i.e., continuum-medial) audio steps.

Analogous to previous research (Rohrer et al., 2025; Bujok et al., 2025; Maran et al., 2025; Cos et al., 2024; Bosker & Peeters, 2021), we expected beat gestures to affect lexical stress perception, also when the emphasised word was embedded in a full sentence.
text.formatted: Analogous to previous research <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Rohrer et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Bujok et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Maran et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Cos et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Bosker & Peeters, 2021)</ref>, we expected beat gestures to affect lexical stress perception, also when the emphasised word was embedded in a full sentence.

text.text: In other words, listeners would be more likely to perceive stress on a syllable when it had a beat gesture aligned to it.
In terms of response times, there was no reason why one beat alignment condition would be associated with faster responses.

However, it was possible that participants would respond faster if the beat gesture alignment matched with the acoustic cues to stress (e.g., a gesture falling on the last syllable of a word with clear final stress).
This would be expressed through an interaction between audio (continuum) step and beat alignment.
The semantic content of the sentence context was also expected to affect the perception of the verb form, as the sentence context provides a reliable cue to the tense of the verb.

Compared to a sentence context without bias, sentences with a present tensebias were expected to elicit higher proportions of yo-responses, as the present-tense verb form (e.g., clasiFIco) is first person singular.
Past tense-biasing sentence contexts would be associated with fewer yo-responses.

Semantic context itself may not be associated with differences in response times; however, it is possible that responses are slower when the sentence context provides an expectation that is later mismatched by either the audio (e.g., clear clasifiCÓ audio following a present tense-biasing sentence context) or the beat gesture (e.g., a beat gesture aligned to the last syllable, cueing clasifiCÓ following a present tense sentence context).

The cue integration framework (Martin, 2016) predicts that cues of different levels of linguistic abstraction are integrated rapidly, so that high-level, semantic cues may also affect the processing of signal-based cues from the subsequent speech signal.

text.text: Moreover, the relative weight by which cues are combined may change depending on their reliability.
As such, it is possible that beat alignment is more influential when acoustic markers of stress are ambiguous, and therefore less reliable (cf. Rohrer et al., 2025; Bujok et al., 2025).

text.text: Furthermore, it is possible that perception processes on the verb form are more efficient if several or all cues are in agreement, providing unified evidence for one member of the minimal stress pair and resulting in faster and less variable responses (see also the cumulative-cue hypothesis; Ambrazaitis & House, 2022).

text.text: If this is the case, we expect to see shorter response times in those cases were acoustic and gestural cues match with each other or with the bias from the sentence context, compared to when different cues communicate different stress patterns.
Lastly, the current study targeted individual differences between listeners in their cue integration strategies through measures of musical aptitude.
To explore this possibility, participants completed two modules of the Profiles of Musical Perception Skills (PROMS) test (Law & Zentner, 2012; Strauss et al., 2024).

text.text: From this test, which contains modules on the perception of various characteristics of music and has undergone extensive validation, the current study tested Rhythm and Accent.
The selection of these modules was motivated by the rhythmic nature of the beat gestures and the fact that musical accent, like lexical stress, involves relative differences in prominence.

Moreover, these specific PROMS test modules have previously been adopted in several studies on gesture and prosody (e.g., Van Maastricht et al., 2022; P. Li et al., 2020; Baills & Prieto, 2023; Baills et al., 2018).

The audiovisual materials for the main experiment were based on sixteen Spanish verbs with a minimal lexical stress pair in their conjugation (e.g., clasiFIco "I classify" vs. clasifiCÓ "(s)he classified").
The verbs were selected based on their high frequencies according to the News on the Web (NOW) component of the Corpus del Español (Davies, 2016).

text.text: All sentences had the same fixed structure, starting with an adverbial phrase, followed by the verb form.
The sentence ended with a direct object noun phrase or an additional adverbial phrase, depending on the transitivity of the verb.
In each sentence set, two sentences started with an adverbial phrase that was exclusively congruent either with the present tense form, or the past tense form.
The third sentence of each set functioned as a neutral sentence context, in which both verb tenses were acceptable.

Two native speakers of Castilian Spanish evaluated all sentences, making sure that the present-and past-biasing sentence contexts were only acceptable with a verb form in the corresponding tense, and that the neutral sentence contexts were acceptable with both tenses.

text.text: The audio component of each recorded sentence was manipulated and pre-tested to ultimately create a 5-step perceptual continuum between the stress patterns of the two verb forms (i.e., stress on the penultimate syllable or on the last syllable).
Specifically, only the final two syllables of the verb form were manipulated to incrementally approach the acoustic characteristics of the verb form with the opposite stress pattern.
For each sentence, the boundaries of the final two syllables of the verb form were annotated manually in Praat.

We then used a Praat script adapted from Rohrer et al. (2025) to linearly interpolate syllable duration, F0 contour, and average syllable intensity between the original recording and the opposite stress pattern.
text.formatted: We then used a Praat script adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Rohrer et al. (2025)</ref> to linearly interpolate syllable duration, F0 contour, and average syllable intensity between the original recording and the opposite stress pattern.

text.text: These characteristics were applied in 10% increments, resulting in 11 audio steps.
For each sentence, the interpolation was applied to the original audio recording.

In other words, the audio of present tense verb forms from the Present and Neutral Sentence Contexts was manipulated towards the acoustic characteristics of the corresponding form in the Past Sentence Context.
Conversely, the audio from the Past Sentence Context verb was manipulated towards the standards of the Present Sentence Context verb form.
The continua were relabelled such that the form with penultimate stress, cuing present tense, was mapped onto step 1 while the form with stress on the last syllable was mapped onto step 11.
With each step in the continuum, the duration, F0 contour and intensity of a syllable changed together, forming a gradual change between the two stress patterns.
See Section 1 of the Supplementary Information in the open data repository for a more detailed description of the acoustic manipulation.
The isolated manipulated verb forms were tested in an auditory-only pretest, with the aim of sampling a uniform perceptual continuum for each sentence.
From each 11-step continuum, the middle 9 steps were tested.
To reduce the duration of the test session, the 16 verbs were divided into two lists of 8, so that every participant would evaluate all stimuli for half of the verbs.

A total of 39 native speakers of Castilian Spanish (M Age = 30.82, SD = 4.66) each evaluated all continua and audio steps for one of the experimental lists (8 verbs * 3 sentence contexts * 9 audio steps = 243 stimuli).
In an online 2-AFC task, they were asked to indicate for each verb form which stress pattern they perceived (e.g., clasiFIco or clasifiCÓ).
These participants were subsequently excluded from the main audiovisual experiment.
Based on the results of the pretest, three audio steps were selected for each sentence to serve as the ambiguous steps in the ultimate 5-step continuum.

This was done by calculating the proportion of responses indicating stress on the penultimate syllable for each audio step and selecting the three audio steps that were cumulatively as close as possible to 75%, 50% (fully ambiguous) and 25% response proportions (Figure 1).

All in all, there were 16 verbs, each with 3 sentence contexts, 5 audio steps, and 2 beat alignment conditions (aligned to the penultimate or ultimate syllable), for a total of 480 unique stimuli.
The stimuli had an average duration of 3.37 seconds (SD = 0.36 s, range: 2.52 -4.24 s).

To avoid an overly long experimental session, the stimuli were again divided into two lists by matching them in terms of lexical frequency according to frequencies reported in the NOW component of the Corpus del Español (Davies, 2016).

text.text: Finally, 24 catch trials were added to each list, in which the beat alignment, auditory stress pattern and sentence context bias all supported the same stress pattern.
In these catch trials, a large white cross was superimposed over the speaker's face.
Participants were asked to respond by pressing the space bar when they encountered a catch trial.
Since catch trials deviated from normal trials only visually, they allowed us to verify whether participants focused visually on the stimuli.

To explore individual variability in the way auditory and visual cues interact in lexical stress perception, the current study employed some modules from the Profile of Music Perception Skills (PROMS) test battery (Law & Zentner, 2012).
text.formatted: To explore individual variability in the way auditory and visual cues interact in lexical stress perception, the current study employed some modules from the Profile of Music Perception Skills (PROMS) test battery <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Law & Zentner, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The test was designed to provide a swift and objective assessment of a listener's ability to discern contrasts in several musical aspects (melody, pitch, timbre, tuning, rhythm, accent, tempo, and loudness).

Each of these aspects is assessed through a module consisting of trials with an AAX structure, where the participant decides if the third fragment is the same as, or different from the first two, which are identical.

The participant responds on a scale with response options "definitely same", "probably same", "don't know", "probably different", and "definitely different", and receives one point in case of a correct 'definitely' response, 0.5 point in case of a correct 'probably' response, and 0 points otherwise.

The test has been extensively validated for use with relatively few items, and with a subset of modules (Strauss et al., 2024; Zentner & Strauss, 2017); in the current study, we tested the modules Accent and Rhythm, as they were expected to be relevant skills specifically for the perception of beat gesture timing and stress perception in general.

text.text: In total, the PROMS scores for a given individual could range from 0 to 18, as there were 18 trials.
Together, the two PROMS test modules took approximately 10 minutes to complete.
The experiment was built and hosted online using Gorilla (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020).
After participants provided consent, they were asked to adjust the audio volume to a comfortable level.
The use of headphones was required and checked using a short intensity-discrimination task (Woods et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The use of headphones was required and checked using a short intensity-discrimination task <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Woods et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The main experiment consisted of a 2-AFC task, where participants saw the video stimulus and selected their response from two options.
A proxy task for the perception of lexical stress was employed, in order not to draw attention to the verb form itself, or one specific (auditory or visual) modality.

Since the two verb forms of the minimal pair are each congruent with a different subject (1st vs. 3rd person singular), we asked our participants to indicate which pronoun (yo "I" or ella "she", congruent with clasiFIco or clasifiCÓ, respectively) they thought fit best with the sentence.
Ella was chosen over él ("he"), to ensure that adjectives with a feminine gender marker matched both the pronoun and the gender of the speaker (in case the "I"-form was perceived).
The response times of the 2-AFC responses were recorded as well, counting from video onset.
Participants had the option to respond at any time once the video stimulus started playing, ensuring the collection of very sensitive response times.
A trial started with a blank screen for 500 ms, followed by a fixation cross for another 500 ms.
Then, the video stimulus started playing automatically.
The video phase of a trial always had a duration of 4250 ms, to accommodate the longest video stimulus (4.24 s).
The entire stimulus was shown, even if a participant responded while it was still playing.
If a response had not been provided during the video phase, the trial continued to a blank answer screen, where participants had another 3000 ms to respond.
Participants were instructed to press F for a yo-response, J for an ella-response, and the spacebar whenever they encountered a catch trial.
The response options were visible throughout the entire trial, and were respectively shown on the left, right, and bottom middle sides of the screen.
There was a brief practice block of 4 trials, including 2 catch trials, using verbs from the other list of the experiment.
The stimuli were offered in a random order.
There were two breaks with a maximum duration of 1 minute and the experiment had a median duration of 36 minutes.
Four participants were removed from the data set because they failed to provide accurate responses to more than one third of the catch trials.
For the remaining data, categorisation responses were recoded with yo responses as 1 and ella responses as 0, to be used as the dependent variable in logistic regression models.
Response times were calculated relative to verb offset, as that was the moment at which all cues to lexical stress were available to the participant.

Responses with negative reaction times (i.e., responses given before verb form offset; 0.83%), as well as outliers outside of 3 SD from the grand mean, were removed from all analyses (1.94% in total).
Three data sets were analysed separately using R (R Core Team, 2026).

For each, a logistic mixed-effects regression model was fit on the categorisation responses, and a linear mixed-effects regression model was fit on the log-transformed response time data, using the lme4 (Bates et al., 2015) and lmerTest packages (Kuznetsova et al., 2017).

text.text: First, to assess whether gesture alignment affects lexical stress perception in full sentences like it does in words in isolation and words in carrier sentences, we analysed the trials with a neutral (nonbiasing) sentence context.

Second, to see how semantic information affected the subsequent processing of acoustic and visual cues to lexical stress, we compared the trials with presenttense and past-tense biasing sentence contexts.
The three sentence context conditions were also analysed all together; this model is available in Section 2 of the Supplementary Information.
The exploratory analyses including measures of musicality were also based on all three contexts combined.

The third data set consisted of the non-biasing sentence context trials of the current study, combined with data of a previous study (Cos et al., 2026), which used exactly the same stimuli and procedure, but exclusively employed non-biasing sentence context trials.

text.text: This comparison was deemed relevant because of the current study's many conflicting stimuli (in which, for example, the sentence context biased towards the present-tense verb form while the acoustic cues indicated the past-tense stress pattern).
The comparison with a data set without such incongruencies allowed us to assess how conflicting stimuli affected stress perception and cue weighting throughout the experiment.
This comparison is included in Section 3 of the Supplementary Information.
Between the models based on categorisation responses and response times, different interactions were of interest.

With respect to the categorisation responses, we expected to find a larger effect of beat alignment when audio was ambiguous, and therefore less reliable (following previous studies; Bujok et al., 2025; Rohrer et al., 2025; Maran et al., 2025).

text.text: In the case of response times, however, there was no reason to expect that one beat alignment condition would be faster than the other when audio was ambiguous.
Instead, we expected that response times would be faster when beat alignment and audio cues provided matching evidence for a specific lexical stress pattern.
The same held for agreement between sentence context and beat alignment, and sentence context and audio continua.

Specifically, when the sentence context provided a bias for the present-tense verb form, we expected faster response times when the suprasegmental cues or gesture alignment indicated stress on the penultimate syllable, compared to when these cues would emphasize the last syllable.

Conversely, when the sentence context biased to the past-tense verb form, we expected faster response times if suprasegmental cues or beat alignment stressed the last syllable rather than the penultimate syllable.

Because of this, the regression models fitted to categorisation responses included interactions between beat alignment and a separate factor for audio ambiguity, whereas models fitted to response times included interactions with the audio continuum itself.

text.text: Lastly, we explored how measures of musicality may affect the use of acoustic and gestural cues to lexical stress.
These analyses were based on all trials, combining the three sentence contexts.
With respect to pronoun selection, the centred PROMS scores did not show a main effect (β = 0.017, SE = 0.066, z = 0.269, p = .788).

However, a significant interaction between PROMS scores and Audio Step (β = -0.023, SE = 0.008, z = -2.728, p = .006) revealed that as Audio Step increased, the proportion of yo-responses showed a steeper decrease for those participants with high, compared to low musicality scores.

This study investigated how acoustic and visual cues to Spanish lexical stress are integrated with each other and with semantic predictions generated by the sentence context.

Specifically, we were interested in the effect of beat gesture alignment on the perception of lexical stress for words that are embedded in full, meaningful sentences, thus taking a step forward in terms of naturalistic language use.

To this end, participants evaluated audiovisual stimuli of a native speaker of Spanish producing complete sentences accompanied by a beat gesture aligned to either one of the two last syllables of the verb form.
They indicated which pronoun they thought fit best as the subject of the sentence, which was taken to reflect which stress pattern they perceived.
All of three cues (suprasegmental cues, gesture alignment, and semantic information) were expected to affect the proportion of responses for the two pronouns.
In addition, we expected to find larger effects of gesture alignment when other cues were less informative (in the case of ambiguous audio or a non-biasing sentence context).
Response times were also analysed, as it was hypothesised that trials with converging cues would be associated with faster response times, compared to trials containing mismatching cues.

Finally, this study explored musical skills as a potential source of individual variation in the integration of audiovisual information from the speech signal, using two modules from the PROMS task (Law & Zentner, 2012).
text.formatted: Finally, this study explored musical skills as a potential source of individual variation in the integration of audiovisual information from the speech signal, using two modules from the PROMS task <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Law & Zentner, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The analyses revealed a robust effect of the acoustic continuum on pronoun selection, confirming the hypothesis that listeners would be sensitive to suprasegmental information during lexical stress perception.

As acoustic markers of stress gradually changed from indicating stress on the penultimate, to stress on the last syllable, participants were ever less likely to select the pronoun matching the penultimate stress pattern.
This held for all sentence contexts, including those that provided a semantic bias to one specific stress pattern.
However, the post-hoc exploratory analysis suggested that there are individual preferences for acoustic or semantic cues, which may indicate a difference in cue weighting strategies.

The response time analyses revealed that participants generally responded faster when stress was clearly marked acoustically, than when it was ambiguous -irrespective of potential biasing information from the sentence context.

On top of this, when the sentence context supported a prediction for a verb tense, and as a result, one specific stress pattern, faster response times were observed when the acoustic cues to stress matched the predicted stress pattern, than when the acoustic cues mismatched it.
Taken together, the results showed that listeners were sensitive to suprasegmental stress information.
Moreover, this cue is informative enough to have an influential weight even when being integrated with linguistic predictions, if those can reliably be made.
In other words, acoustic cues are not overruled by semantic information in lexical stress perception.
When it comes to pronoun selection, the analysis of pronoun responses provided no evidence for an effect of gesture alignment -contrary to our second hypothesis.

At least during a task of pronoun selection, a beat gesture aligning with either one of the two last syllables did not result in significantly more responses of the pronoun matching the stress pattern indicated by the gesture.

In this regard, the results of the current study seem to mismatch a range of studies that found such a gesture alignment effect on stress pattern categorisation for isolated words, both in Spanish and Dutch (Bujok et al., 2025; Rohrer et al., 2025; Maran et al., 2025; Cos et al., 2024), or for words in carrier sentences (Bosker & Peeters, 2021).

text.text: Given the more naturalistic nature of the stimuli of the current study, which featured complete and meaningful utterances, these findings may be taken to suggest that the visual cue of beat gestures is weighted relatively lightly when it comes to the perception of lexical stress in complete utterances, at least when going by the behavioural responses.
The apparent reduction in the effect of gesture alignment is not straightforward to explain.
One explanation might be the task adopted in the current study, which probed stress perception indirectly by asking listeners to select the pronoun that best fit the sentence.
Previous studies, on the other hand, simply asked participants which member of the minimal pair they perceived (in the case of Rohrer et al., 2025; e.g., HAblo or haBLÓ, including the formatting).
text.formatted: Previous studies, on the other hand, simply asked participants which member of the minimal pair they perceived (in the case of <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Rohrer et al., 2025</ref>; e.g., HAblo or haBLÓ, including the formatting).

text.text: The current study deviated from this paradigm to avoid explicitly drawing attention to the verb form as well as the acoustic modality, as participants might have strategically disregarded the rest of the sentence (including its biasing context) after getting used to the structure of the stimuli.
It is therefore possible that the additional morphological evaluation of which pronoun better suited the perceived stress pattern obscured a categorisation effect.
There are several studies that do report effects of beat gestures for words embedded in sentences.

However, these studies have focused mostly on phrasal stress, and how beat gestures may be used to emphasize words (i.e., not individual syllables), marking them as important or putting them in focus (Krahmer & Swerts, 2007; Leonard & Cummins, 2011; Dimitrova et al., 2016; Biau & Soto-Faraco, 2013).

text.text: In these strands of research, beat gestures seem to have a meaningful effect, also when the words they are aligned to are embedded in sentences.

As such, it is possible that beat gestures, in more naturalistic situations, are primarily interpreted as markers of information structure or even as paralinguistic markers, signalling that challenging or unexpected speech elements are coming up.

A related explanation is that beat gestures are a less reliable cue to lexical stress because it is more difficult to determine where exactly the gesture is aligned at the syllable level compared to the word level.

That is, the temporal difference between aligning a beat gesture to one or the other syllable within a word is much smaller than the difference between aligning it to one or the other word in a sentence.

Indeed, the current study, featuring a more naturalistic speech rate compared to studies using isolated words, exhibited a much smaller timing difference between beat conditions compared to the only other study on beat gestures and lexical stress in Spanish (Rohrer et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Indeed, the current study, featuring a more naturalistic speech rate compared to studies using isolated words, exhibited a much smaller timing difference between beat conditions compared to the only other study on beat gestures and lexical stress in Spanish <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Rohrer et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In this older study, the timing difference between beat alignment conditions was on average 303 ms, compared to 170 ms in the present study.
The tighter timescale may have made it more difficult to determine where exactly the beat gesture was aligned.
In turn, the cue of beat gesture alignment may have been treated as less reliable, causing it to be weighted only lightly compared to previous studies.

Importantly, it is unlikely that the participants were unable to determine where the gesture was aligned at all, given the difference in response times between beat alignment conditions (discussed below in greater detail).

Future studies may investigate whether the timescale is indeed an important factor in cue weighting, or if beat gestures naturally pertain primarily to higher-level prosodic or pragmatic domains (such as focus marking or 'warning' for unexpected elements in the speech signal).

As opposed to the pronoun selection responses, the response time analyses revealed that for trials with a sentence context that supported a prediction for one specific stress pattern, participants generally responded faster when the gesture was aligned to the syllable that matched the stressed syllable of the prediction.

For example, in the case of present-tense biasing elements like En este momento "At the moment", creating a prediction for a presenttense (clasiFIco) stress pattern, participants responded faster if there was a beat gesture aligned to the penultimate syllable instead of the last syllable.

These findings indicate that the listeners were sensitive to the syllable-level timing of the beat gesture, even if this cue was not weighted heavily enough to determine the listener's categorisation response.
There are several studies that showed that listeners are faster to respond to multimodal vs. unimodal utterances.

For example, it has been shown that questions are answered faster if they are accompanied by semantically constraining gestures (including iconic and deictic gestures; Holler et al., 2018; ter Bekke et al., 2024), and that participants were faster at indicating whether they felt addressed or not when a stimulus was combined with an iconic gesture (Nagels et al., 2015).

text.text: With respect to lexical access, it has been shown that participants were faster to relate primes and targets when the stimuli contained iconic gestures and speech that matched, rather than mismatched (Kelly et al., 2010).

text.text: Because the current study did not feature any stimuli without gestures altogether, it cannot be determined whether matching gesture timing facilitated word recognition, or if a mismatching gesture timing disrupted it.
Nevertheless, the current study does show that listeners are sensitive to the subtle difference in timing of beat gestures when it comes to perceiving lexical stress.

Taken together, it seems that, also in naturalistic sentences, native Spanish listeners are sensitive to (mis)matching beat gesture timing, even if this cue is perhaps weighted so lightly that it is unable to alter the listener's ultimate pronoun response.
The current study only used minimal lexical stress pairs, and the candidate syllables for bearing lexical stress were always adjacent.

As such, it is possible that beat gestures have an even larger impact on word perception in cases where the candidate syllables to lexical stress are non-adjacent, as is the case for many embedded words and non-minimal pairs (e.g., Spanish
CAra "face" vs. caraMElo "caramel", Cutler et al., 2004).

text.text: It is also possible that gesture alignment would be weighed more heavily in the cue integration process if other (e.g., suprasegmental) cues are unreliable or even absent, such as in noisy communicative settings or accented (learner's) speech.

On the other hand, it is likely that natural speech exhibits larger variability in gesture-speech alignment (see Loehr, 2012), which may counteract the potential increased reliability of gestural cues in noise.

text.text: Finally, in everyday communication, a speaker may employ a range of simultaneous visual signals to convey stress and emphasis, combining gestures with head and eyebrow movements (Holler & Levinson, 2019).

text.text: As such, the current results -obtained with stimuli isolating the contribution of particular visual cues -may underestimate the potential of visual signals to communicate lexical stress in real conversations.
Lastly, the exploratory analyses using measures of musicality revealed that participants with higher PROMS scores exhibited a stronger effect of suprasegmental cues on pronoun selection.
Moreover, listeners with stronger musical skills were faster at responding whenever the acoustic cues to stress were clear, compared to participants with lower scores.

Several other studies reported that stronger musical skills correlate with higher accuracy in lexical stress discrimination when it is clearly marked (see Jansen et al., 2023), though most of these studies focus on language learners -possibly because native speakers are expected to achieve overwhelmingly high accuracies (e.g., Podlipský et al., 2026; Nayak et al., 2022; Schwab & García, 2026; Degrave, 2017).

text.text: None of these studies have tested native listeners at perceiving ambiguously marked stress, however; the current study tentatively suggests that in native listeners, musicality may provide an advantage in lexical stress processing, but only when lexical stress is clearly marked rather than ambiguous.
This finding requires more rigorous investigation.
The PROMS scores of musicality never interacted with any effect involving beat gesture alignment.

This study investigated audiovisual lexical stress perception in native speakers of Spanish, implementing stress through suprasegmental cues and beat gestures, for words embedded in full, meaningful sentences.
Crossing these cues enabled us to investigate how multimodal cues are integrated during lexical stress perception.

The results revealed that Spanish listeners are sensitive to acoustic cues when it comes to lexical stress perception of words in full sentences, even in the face of clear biases from the sentence context.
Moreover, when combined with a semantic prediction, responses were faster when a beat gesture was aligned to the expected, rather than the unexpected syllable.

Unlike previous studies using isolated words and unpredictive contexts, the gesture cue was not strong enough to change the listener's response, suggesting that the visual cue of gestures receives only limited weight in cue integration when it comes to lexical stress perception in connected speech.

Future studies may investigate the circumstances under which visual cues exhibit a more influential weighting in cue integration, including speech in noise (reducing the reliability of acoustic cues), at lower speech rates (potentially increasing the reliability of gestural cues), or with different populations (e.g., second language learners who may benefit more from a transparent marker of lexical stress).

Conversely, if beat gesture alignment primarily affects the process leading up to the response more so than the response itself, it may be interesting to see how beat gestures affect the neurological processes behind lexical stress processing.
